precepts.text: Keturah has six sons from Abraham, and Midian is one of them.
precepts.point: Now they couldn't explain Joseph not being there, so they concocted the story that a wild animal killed Joseph, and dipped the coat of many colors in the blood of a kid of the goats. The brothers were so envious of Joseph. Envy will have you do some evil stuff.
precepts.why:
When Joseph’s brothers sat down to eat bread, they saw “a company of Ishmeelites came from Gilead with their camels bearing spicery and balm and myrrh, going to carry it down to Egypt.” Judah said, “What profit is it if we slay our brother, and conceal his blood? Come, and let us sell him to the Ishmeelites.” Then the verse changes names: “Then there passed by Midianites merchantmen; and they drew and lifted up Joseph out of the pit, and sold Joseph to the Ishmeelites for twenty pieces of silver.”

There are always questions about the Midianites and the Ishmaelites. Genesis 25 shows who the Midianites were: “Then again Abraham took a wife, and her name was Keturah. And she bare him Zimran, and Jokshan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah.” Keturah had six sons by Abraham, and Midian is one of them. The chapter goes on to his sons: “And the sons of Midian; Ephah, and Epher, and Hanoch, and Abida, and Eldaah. All these were the children of Keturah.”

So the Midianites are Abraham’s children through Keturah, just as the Ishmaelites are Abraham’s children through Hagar. They were working together and roaming the land together, all Abraham’s kids, and they looked very similar. That is why the story says Ishmaelites, then Midianites, then “the Midianites sold him into Egypt unto Potiphar,” and then in Genesis 39 Potiphar “bought him of the hands of the Ishmeelites.” It is not a contradiction; these groups were together.

precepts.text: Abraham had Ishmael from Hagar the Egyptian, and Ishmael had twelve princes according to their nations. Abraham's children from Keturah and Abraham's children from Hagar always lived together and worked together.
precepts.point: Now they couldn't explain Joseph not being there, so they concocted the story that a wild animal killed Joseph, and dipped the coat of many colors in the blood of a kid of the goats. The brothers were so envious of Joseph. Envy will have you do some evil stuff.
precepts.why:
Genesis 37 names both groups in the sale of Joseph: the Midianites drew him out of the pit and “sold Joseph to the Ishmeelites for twenty pieces of silver,” and later “the Midianites sold him into Egypt unto Potiphar.” Genesis 25:12 shows who the Ishmaelites were: “Now these are the generations of Ishmael, Abraham’s son, whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah’s handmaid, bare unto Abraham.”

Abraham had Ishmael from Hagar, and Ishmael had sons as well: Nebajoth the firstborn, “and Kedar, and Adbeel, and Mibsam, And Mishma, and Dumah, and Massa, Hadar, and Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah.” “These are the sons of Ishmael, and these are their names, by their towns, and by their castles; twelve princes according to their nations.”

Abraham’s children from Keturah and Abraham’s children from Hagar always lived together and worked together. So when a company of Ishmaelites comes by carrying spices down to Egypt and Midianite merchantmen are among them, it is one caravan of Abraham’s other children traveling side by side.

Meanwhile the brothers, so envious of Joseph, dipped his coat of many colours in the blood of a kid of the goats and let Jacob believe “an evil beast hath devoured him.” Reuben had suggested the pit so he could come back and save him, and when he returned, “Joseph was not in the pit; and he rent his clothes.” Envy will have you do evil things. Remember Reuben’s character; it plays a part later.

precepts.text: A witness that does not utter what he has seen bears his own iniquity; Joseph uttered the evil report according to that law.
precepts.point: Joseph brought unto his father the evil report of his brethren. That was law, not tale bearing: if a soul hear swearing and be a witness and do not utter it, he shall bear his iniquity. The law was already around, and Joseph kept it.
precepts.why:
“And if a soul sin, and hear the voice of swearing, and is a witness, whether he hath seen or known of it; if he do not utter it, then he shall bear his iniquity.” A witness that does not utter what he has seen bears his own iniquity.

So when Joseph “brought unto his father their evil report”, that was law, not tale bearing. The law was already around, and Joseph kept it by uttering what he had seen.

precepts.text: The Most High multiplies visions and uses similitudes by the ministry of the prophets.
precepts.point: His brethren understood the dream, that he should reign over them, and hated him yet the more for his dreams and for his words.
precepts.why:
“I have also spoken by the prophets, and I have multiplied visions, and used similitudes, by the ministry of the prophets.” The Lord speaks by the prophets in visions and similitudes.

Joseph's dream is one of them: sheaves in the field, and “your sheaves stood round about, and made obeisance to my sheaf.” His brethren understood the similitude, that he should reign over them, and hated him yet the more for his dreams and for his words.

precepts.text: The vision of dreams is the resemblance of one thing to another; the sheaf stood for Joseph and the sheaves for his brethren.
precepts.point: His brethren understood the dream, that he should reign over them, and hated him yet the more for his dreams and for his words.
precepts.why:
“The vision of dreams is the resemblance of one thing to another, even as the likeness of a face to a face.”

That is how to read Joseph's dream. The sheaf stood for Joseph and the sheaves for his brethren; one thing resembles another, as a face to a face. His brethren read it right: “Shalt thou indeed reign over us? or shalt thou indeed have dominion over us?” And they hated him yet the more.

precepts.text: The woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars, figures Israel and her tribes.
precepts.point: The dream came true. In the famine the whole house of Jacob came down to Joseph in Egypt, and he placed them in the best of the land and nourished them with bread; they bowed to the one the Most High had set over them.
precepts.why:
“a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and upon her head a crown of twelve stars”. The woman is Israel and the twelve stars are the tribes.

The same figures are in Joseph's dream: “the sun and the moon and the eleven stars made obeisance to me.” Jacob interpreted it at once: “Shall I and thy mother and thy brethren indeed come to bow down ourselves to thee to the earth?” The sun, the moon and the stars are the house of Israel.

precepts.text: The daughter of Zion is likened to a comely and delicate woman; the woman of the vision is Israel.
precepts.point: The dream came true. In the famine the whole house of Jacob came down to Joseph in Egypt, and he placed them in the best of the land and nourished them with bread; they bowed to the one the Most High had set over them.
precepts.why:
“I have likened the daughter of Zion to a comely and delicate woman.” The daughter of Zion is the nation of Israel, and she is likened to a woman.

That is who the woman clothed with the sun with the crown of twelve stars is: Israel, and the twelve stars her tribes. Joseph's dream of the sun, the moon and the eleven stars bowing to him is the same picture of the house of Jacob, which Jacob read at once as himself, Joseph's mother and his brethren.

precepts.text: Joseph placed his father and his brethren in the best of the land and nourished them; the dream was fulfilled.
precepts.point: The dream came true. In the famine the whole house of Jacob came down to Joseph in Egypt, and he placed them in the best of the land and nourished them with bread; they bowed to the one the Most High had set over them.
precepts.why:
“And Joseph placed his father and his brethren, and gave them a possession in the land of Egypt, in the best of the land, in the land of Rameses, as Pharaoh had commanded. And Joseph nourished his father, and his brethren, and all his father’s household, with bread”.

The dream came true. In the famine the whole house of Jacob came down to Joseph in Egypt, and he placed them in the best of the land and nourished them with bread. The sun, the moon and the eleven stars bowed to the one the Most High had set over them.

precepts.text: Consuming envy has no fellowship with wisdom; the brothers' envy put wisdom away from them.
precepts.point: His brethren envied him, but his father observed the saying. Envy consumes a man, and such a man shall have no fellowship with wisdom; when envy takes over, wisdom leaves.
precepts.why:
“Neither will I go with consuming envy; for such a man shall have no fellowship with wisdom.” Envy is consuming: it eats a man up. And a man consumed by it has no fellowship with wisdom; when envy takes over, wisdom leaves.

That is what happened to Joseph’s brethren. “And his brethren envied him”: their envy put wisdom away from them, and with wisdom gone there was nothing to hold back what they went on to do to their brother. Their father, on the other hand, “observed the saying.”

precepts.text: Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer, and no murderer hath eternal life abiding in him.
precepts.point: Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer. Inner hatred, given room, plots death; that is why the law says thou shalt not hate thy brother in thine heart.
precepts.why:
“Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer: and ye know that no murderer hath eternal life abiding in him.” The brethren had not yet laid a hand on Joseph when they saw him afar off, but in their hearts they had already killed him: “Come now therefore, and let us slay him, and cast him into some pit.” Inner hatred, given room, plots death.

That is why the law says thou shalt not hate thy brother in thine heart. The hatred was there first, and the conspiring to slay him came out of it. It is the same spirit Cain had, and the same spirit Esau had: “Behold, this dreamer cometh.”

And no murderer hath eternal life abiding in him. The hating of a brother is not a small thing; it is murder in the sight of God, and it costs a man eternal life.

precepts.text: Neither deal falsely, neither lie one to another; the brothers broke that law before their father.
precepts.point: The Midianites sold him in Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard.
precepts.why:
“Ye shall not steal, neither deal falsely, neither lie one to another.” The brothers did exactly that before their father. They took Joseph’s coat, dipped it in the blood of a kid of the goats, and sent it to Jacob with the words “This have we found: know now whether it be thy son’s coat or no.” They dealt falsely, and they let their father believe that “an evil beast hath devoured him.”

That lie against the law is what put Jacob in sackcloth, mourning for his son many days and refusing to be comforted: “For I will go down into the grave unto my son mourning.”

precepts.text: Ye thought evil against me, but God meant it unto good, to save much people alive.
precepts.point: The Midianites sold him in Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard.
precepts.why:
Joseph told his brethren later what was really behind it all: “But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.” The brothers meant evil when they sold him and dipped his coat in blood; God meant it unto good.

That is why Jacob could not see through the lie. The thing was of the Lord. Had Joseph never gone down to Egypt, the whole house of Israel would have died in the famine. So the Midianites selling him “into Egypt unto Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh’s, and captain of the guard” was God sending him ahead to save much people alive.
